record.paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
record.original_question: Can the transfer of kinetic energy into shell or membrane vibrations explain the observed energy loss in impacts of hollow balls and inflated sports balls? A satisfactory answer should distinguish shell-dominated balls with storage number St much greater than 1, such as table-tennis balls, from gas-dominated inflated balls with storage number St much less than 1, such as basketballs, and should determine whether the relevant vibration amplitudes and frequencies are large enough to account for the measured dissipated energy.

evidence.quote: Dissipation could occur in the shell through ball vibrations as suggested by Cross (2014). We have here to separate the vibrations in two different origins: (i) the vibration of elastic shells (i.e. the elasticity of the shell stores the energy, St ≫ 1, e.g tennis-table balls) and (ii) the vibration of inflated membranes (i.e. similar to the model developed in the Section 2 where all the elesticity is in the gas and all the mass in the membrane, St ≪ 1, e.g basket balls).
For a basket ball, A ∼ 1 mm, f ∼ 1.7 102 Hz, one obtains Ed,vibrations = 9.5 J. Thus, the energy lost by vibrations is smaller than the one observed experimentally.

For vibrations of inflated balls, we propose to equip the ball with a accelerometer to measure microscopic vibrations of the shell. This accelerometer should have a frequency response higher than the first mode of vibration of the ball (10 4 Hz for a tennis table ball). Its pass band should also be in the range of the frequency of vibration of the ball. For large balls, direct optical measurements should be able to give the amplitude of vibration (∼ 1 mm). These vibrations would correspond to the momentum flux force dissipation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a hollow ball of mass $m$, radius $R$, and shell thickness $h$, made of a material with Young's modulus $E$, possibly inflated with an internal gas at gauge pressure $P$. Define the dimensionless storage number
$$\mathrm{St} = \frac{E h}{P R},$$
which compares the elastic stiffness stored in the shell to the stiffness stored in the enclosed gas. Two limiting regimes are distinguished:
(i) shell-dominated balls with $\mathrm{St} \gg 1$ (e.g. table-tennis balls), where elastic energy is stored predominantly in the bending/stretching of the elastic shell, and
(ii) gas-dominated inflated balls with $\mathrm{St} \ll 1$ (e.g. basketballs), where elastic energy is stored predominantly in the compressed gas while inertia resides in the membrane.

When such a ball impacts a rigid surface with incoming kinetic energy $E_k$, a fraction is dissipated, producing a coefficient of restitution $e<1$. One proposed dissipation channel is the transfer of kinetic energy into vibrational modes of the shell or membrane, with characteristic amplitude $A$ and dominant frequency $f$, giving a vibrational energy of order
$$E_{d,\mathrm{vib}} \sim m\,(2\pi f A)^2.$$

Problem. Develop a quantitative model of vibrational energy dissipation during the impact of a hollow or inflated ball that:
(a) treats the two regimes $\mathrm{St}\gg 1$ and $\mathrm{St}\ll 1$ separately, predicting the dominant mode amplitude $A$ and frequency $f$ as functions of $m, R, h, E, P$ and impact velocity $v$;
(b) determines whether the predicted $E_{d,\mathrm{vib}}$ is sufficient to account for the experimentally measured energy loss $(1-e^2)E_k$ in impacts of, in particular, table-tennis balls and basketballs;
(c) identifies the parameter ranges in which shell/membrane vibrations are the leading dissipation mechanism, versus ranges where other mechanisms (gas viscous losses, contact friction, plastic deformation) must dominate.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns whether shell/membrane vibrational energy can quantitatively account for the observed coefficient-of-restitution losses in impacts of hollow and inflated balls. Order-of-magnitude estimates suggest vibrational energy is insufficient for inflated balls such as basketballs, but no comprehensive theory across both St ≫ 1 and St ≪ 1 regimes appears to have been established, and direct accelerometer/optical measurements proposed to test it have not been definitively reported. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
status_evidence.snippet: Lists vibrational energy loss as one of several open mechanisms and proposes future accelerometer/optical measurements.
status_evidence.claim: The vibrational dissipation mechanism is posed as an open question.
